doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
title: No writing in jail, and teaching novices
summary: Jail did not inspire composing, and McLean taught beginners any instrument from a book.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Did you have – did you – do any of your compositions emanate from your time there? Did you do any writing while you were there?

No, man. It wasn’t an environment that I was inspired to do anything in. Just play every day. Being locked away like that, it’s – you always hear about some guy, “plays saxophone. He was locked away for five years, man. He ain’t been doing nothing but practicing in there for five years.” He ain’t going to have much to do when he comes
out. He’ll have a lot of technique and everything, but his head, his environment, keeps him from being so creative.
In the circumstance when you were teaching, were these novices? Or were there other talented musicians that you had a chance to work with, when you had the job?

No, they were novices. I was even teaching trombone, any instrument. I’d just have a book. “I want to play trombone.” “Okay, this is A and this is B,” like that. “You go practice those tunes. I’ll see you tomorrow. Okay? Next.” That’s what it was like.
